title: decide whether plan approval must leave an active graph revision: ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT is the ORDINARY journey state and 15 production readers resolve against it
description:
MEASURED at HEAD f6e97a6b on 2026-09-12 by architect-76be3b8c while planning task-c7a66b703c73466eba616a7dc6fbef23. Filed as that row's DoD 4 split — c7a66b70 makes the policy-risk writer's silence OBSERVABLE, and explicitly does NOT decide this, because this question's blast radius is every consumer of `readCurrentActiveGraph` rather than the one writer. THIS ROW EXISTS; c7a66b70's plan names it by id rather than promising a filing.

THE QUESTION. `approval-activation.ts` Path B has no graph-revision activation leg of its own. It reads `readCurrentActiveGraph(store, request.projectId)` at :191 and, when that answers ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT, supplies `subject: null` to the policy-risk writer — which then refuses POLICY_RISK_SUBJECT_UNAVAILABLE and records no risk authority. Measured over a completed `journeyWorld("SUBMITTED")`: `readCurrentActiveGraph(store, project-1)` answers ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT @ ACTIVE_GRAPH_PROJECTION and `enumerateAggregateIdsByPrefix("policy-risk:sha256:")` returns ZERO records. ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT is not an edge case here; it is what the ordinary journey leaves behind.

The corroborating history: `gates-unattended-fixtures.ts` used to FABRICATE an active graph revision after approval, with a comment saying it did so precisely because the journey leaves none. task-510340a346c24615a2177c2db9a85782 deleted that fabrication. The fixture was compensating for this gap for as long as it existed.

WHY THIS IS NOT A ONE-LINE ADDITION. If plan approval should activate a graph revision, that changes what fifteen production call sites resolve against. Enumerated at HEAD so the planner starts from a list rather than a grep — CLASSIFYING each one is this row's work, and NOT yet done:

    activation/activation-budget-derivation.ts:164
    bootstrap/policy-risk-reader.ts:120
    budget/budget-durable-binding.ts:119
    budget/budget-settlement-application.ts:104
    daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts:440      (port wiring)
    planning/approval-activation.ts:191             (the site in question)
    planning/expansion-release-selector.ts:81
    planning/expansion-request-current-authority.ts:182
    planning/graph-query.ts:235                     (through the port)
    planning/graph-supersede-facts.ts:204
    planning/node-closure-reader.ts:134
    planning/supersession-preparation-ledger.ts:82  (RELEASE_ACTIVATION_EVIDENCE)
    planning/supersession-preparation-service.ts:83
    work/foundation-context-matrix.ts:134
    work/foundation-dispatch-derivation.ts:143

Test-side seeding also exists and must not be mistaken for production behaviour: `activation/activation-world-fixtures.ts:346,403` and `budget/budget-ledger-fixtures.ts`.

READ BEFORE DECIDING. `planning/graph-revision-activation-leg.ts:19` records that the leg "had no production caller at all and `readCurrentActiveGraph` could never answer for a real" project, and :132 discusses the fail-closed direction. That module may already be the mechanism this row needs to WIRE rather than build. `graph-activation-service.ts:245` takes the opposite approach deliberately — it derives the risk subject from the TRANSITION rather than from `readCurrentActiveGraph`, because the graph is not active yet at that point — and that comment is the best statement on the tree of why the two paths differ. Do not unify them without answering it.

THE DECISION IS THE DELIVERABLE, and either answer is a valid outcome. If approval SHOULD activate a revision, this row wires it with every consumer above classified. If it should NOT, this row says so in `approval-activation.ts`'s header in the code's own voice, and ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT-after-approval becomes a documented, intended state rather than an unexamined one — which is worth landing on its own, because today nothing on the tree says which it is.

VERIFY BEFORE PLANNING — this description is stale by default. Re-run `grep -rn 'readCurrentActiveGraph' apps/daemon/src --include=*.ts | grep -v test` and compare against the fifteen above; a changed list means a consumer moved and the classification must follow it.
definitionOfDone: The decision is RECORDED IN CODE, not only in the row: `approval-activation.ts`'s header states whether plan approval leaves an active graph revision and why, in the same voice as the surrounding modules. A reader of Path B can tell which of the two answers is intended without consulting the board.

All fifteen production `readCurrentActiveGraph` call sites listed in the description are re-grepped at implementation time and each is CLASSIFIED in the plan or the header as (a) unaffected, (b) behaviour-changed by this row and covered by an arm, or (c) explicitly out of scope with the reason. A site that is merely listed is not classified.

If the answer is that approval SHOULD activate a revision: an arm drives the production approval path over a real `journeyWorld("SUBMITTED")` and asserts `readCurrentActiveGraph` answers OK afterwards, AND asserts the downstream effect that motivated this row — `enumerateAggregateIdsByPrefix("policy-risk:sha256:")` is non-empty and `readPolicyRisk` answers a real tier rather than POLICY_RISK_RECORD_MISSING.

If the answer is that it should NOT: an arm pins ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT after an ordinary approval as the INTENDED state, asserting the code AND the layer (ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT @ ACTIVE_GRAPH_PROJECTION) per this epic's rail on refusals, so a future change that silently starts activating one reds here.

`planning/graph-revision-activation-leg.ts` is either wired by this row or its header is updated to say why it still has no production caller. It must not be left asserting a state of affairs this row has moved past.
Non-vacuity: the chosen arm is proven to fail when the behaviour is reverted — quote the red with its code and layer, not merely a count change.

`pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` EXIT 0 with the `Test Files N passed (N)` count line quoted. This row adds no runtime command kind, so no control-room leg and no digest-mirror census is owed — confirm that at plan time rather than assuming it.

implementationPlan.description: CONFIRM THE FOUR FACTS THAT DECIDE THE ANSWER - read only, no edits. The owner delegated this decision to the architect and I answered NO on the evidence below; your job in this step is to try to falsify it, not to confirm it. (1) The ROUTING TABLE: `daemon-command-graph-edges.ts:26` records `graph.approve -> activateApprovedGraph (task-eacea969)`, and `daemon-command-graph-approve.ts:168` makes that call. (2) THAT surface always activates: `graph-activation-service.ts:240-243` says "The revision leg is ALWAYS present - an activation that activates no graph is not a state this surface can express." (3) The approval path is a DIFFERENT command: `approval-intent-activation.ts:228` calls `activateInitialGraphWithApprovalReplay`, whose durable event is `GoalExecutionEnabled` on the GOAL (`approval-activation.ts:175-183`) - it enables a goal's execution, it does not activate a graph revision. (4) THE JOURNEY NEVER RUNS graph.approve: `git grep -In 'graph\.approve\|graphApprove' -- apps/daemon/src/gates-journey-fixtures.ts apps/daemon/src/gates-unattended-fixtures.ts` returns ZERO. That is why `readCurrentActiveGraph` answers ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT on the ordinary journey, and why `gates-unattended-fixtures.ts` used to FABRICATE a revision. If any of the four is false at HEAD, STOP and moe.report_blocked - the answer changes with them. All four are SOURCE READS by architect-76be3b8c, not runs; label them that way if you cite them.
implementationPlan.note:

(1) ROUTING TABLE. `daemon-command-graph-edges.ts:26` reads `graph.approve -> activateApprovedGraph (task-eacea969)`, inside a header enumerating the five graph MUTATION kinds. The call is real: `daemon-command-graph-approve.ts:168` `return activateApprovedGraph(graphHandlerContext(store, ledger, request), activation);`. CONFIRMED.

(2) THAT SURFACE ALWAYS ACTIVATES. `graph-activation-service.ts:240-241`: "The revision leg is ALWAYS present — an activation that activates no graph is not a state this surface can express". Corroborated structurally at :242-244 — `extraLegs` is `[transition.leg, root.leg, slotLeg]` on GENESIS and `[transition.leg, slotLeg]` otherwise; `transition.leg` is unconditional on BOTH arms. CONFIRMED.

(3) THE APPROVAL PATH IS A DIFFERENT COMMAND. `approval-intent-activation.ts:228` `return activateInitialGraphWithApprovalReplay(context, input, input.sourceFences);`. Its durable event is `approval-activation.ts:173-182`: `aggregateId: input.goalId`, `eventType: "GoalExecutionEnabled"`. It enables a GOAL's execution; it writes no graph-revision aggregate. CONFIRMED.

(4) THE JOURNEY NEVER RUNS graph.approve. `git grep -In 'graph\.approve\|graphApprove' -- apps/daemon/src/gates-journey-fixtures.ts apps/daemon/src/gates-unattended-fixtures.ts` returned ZERO lines. CONFIRMED. None of the four is false, so the NO answer stands and I do not report blocked.

- `git grep -n 'buildGraphRevisionActivationLeg'` over apps/daemon/src + packages + adapters: exactly ONE production caller, `graph-transition-legs.ts:102` (its own definition at graph-revision-activation-leg.ts:217; the only other hits are two .test.ts files). So the leg is not reachable from a second surface.
- `git grep -n 'activateApprovedGraph'`: exactly ONE production caller, `daemon-command-graph-approve.ts:168`. Every other hit is a .test.ts, a *-test-fixtures.ts, or a comment.
- A SECOND production writer of graph-revision events DOES exist and step 1 did not name it: `graph-supersede-legs.ts:113` drives `reduceGraphRevision` on the `graph.supersede` path. It does NOT weaken the answer — supersede REQUIRES an already-active graph (`graph-supersede-facts.ts:204` reads `readCurrentActiveGraph` to find the predecessor), so it can move the active revision but can never create the first one. Recorded here for step 8 question (1).

implementationPlan.description: CLASSIFY ALL FIFTEEN READERS - this is DoD 2 and it is the step that could still overturn the answer. Listing a site is not classifying it. THE OVERTURN CONDITION, stated so you do not have to judge it alone: if any site falls in (b) - a production reader that is actually wrong or dead when the graph is absent, not merely fail-closed - then ABSENT is not a benign intended state and the NO answer is in doubt. Do NOT change behaviour in that case and do NOT quietly switch to YES; record the finding and moe.report_blocked so the decision returns to the architect and the owner. Fail-closed handling is NOT breakage: a reader that refuses cleanly on ABSENT is evidence FOR the answer, not against it.

TALLY: 13 in (a), 2 in (c), 0 in (b). Every (a) preserves the projection's own code AND layer rather than restamping it into local vocabulary — that is a tree-wide convention, and a tree that consistently forwards ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT with its layer is a tree that treats it as a legitimate answer. Not one reader assumes ok, dereferences without a guard, or silently defaults.

implementationPlan.description: RECORD THE DECISION IN CODE - DoD 1, and the actual deliverable of this row. In `approval-activation.ts`'s header, state in the module's own voice that plan approval DELIBERATELY does not leave an active graph revision, and why: `graph.approve` owns that transition and always commits the revision leg, while this path's durable effect is `GoalExecutionEnabled` on the goal. Name what ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT after an ordinary approval MEANS - the journey has not run `graph.approve`, not that something failed - so the next reader of `readCurrentActiveGraph` at :191 stops reading it as a defect. State the consequence that motivated the parent row: because the graph is absent, the policy-risk subject is null on this path; note that the risk leg refuses EARLIER than that anyway (see step 5's note) so the subject is not what omits the record. A reader of Path B must be able to tell which of the two answers is intended WITHOUT consulting the board.

THE ARM LANDED — DoD 4. New suite `apps/daemon/src/planning/approval-activation-graph-absence.test.ts` (103 lines, 2 arms).

RUN: `npx vitest run --root . --config package.json src/planning/approval-activation-graph-absence.test.ts` from apps/daemon -> `Test Files 1 passed (1)` / `Tests 2 passed (2)`, exit 0. NONZERO executed count, so the leg is not vacuous.

ARM (a) — the pinned decision. Drives `journeyWorld("SUBMITTED")`, the real production journey (bound PRD -> revision -> Gate 1 -> design -> submit -> production `approvePlan` -> landed -> published -> preview receipt). Asserts THREE things, in order:
  1. THE APPROVAL COMMITTED, so "nothing ran" cannot masquerade as "correctly absent". Two independent durable facts: `store.readEvents(GOAL_ID).filter(e => e.eventType === "GoalExecutionEnabled")` has length exactly 1 — the decision's own primary leg, the very event the header names — and `activeCompiledGraphs(store, PROJECT_ID, new Set(["EXECUTION_ENABLED"]))` contains GOAL_ID, a production reader that admits only enabled goals.
  2. THE MECHANISM one layer below the projection: `enumerateAggregateIdsByPrefix(graphRevisionAggregateId(PROJECT_ID, ""))` is `[]`. No revision leg was committed at all. Deliberate belt-and-braces — the projection verdict alone would stay green if a revision were committed in a NON-ACTIVE lifecycle, which is a different world this row did not decide.
  3. THE CODE AND THE LAYER, per epic rail 4: `toMatchObject({ code: "ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT", layer: ACTIVE_GRAPH_PROJECTION_LAYER, ok: false })`. `ok: false` alone would stay green on ACTIVE_GRAPH_SPLIT_BRAIN or ACTIVE_GRAPH_BODY_UNAVAILABLE, which mean the OPPOSITE — a revision IS there and something is wrong with it. The layer comes from the exported constant, not a string literal, so a rename cannot leave the assertion silently pointing at a dead value.

ARM (b) — the in-suite positive control, and it SURVIVES THE COMMIT rather than living in a deleted probe (evidence rail's preferred form). comments.content:
HARD CONSTRAINT DISCOVERED AFTER THIS ROW WAS FILED — measured by worker-a1cf5270 on task-c7a66b703c73466eba616a7dc6fbef23 at 2026-09-11T23:16Z, recorded here by architect-76be3b8c. READ THIS BEFORE PLANNING; it narrows one of this row's two valid answers.

THE ORDINARY JOURNEY'S PLAN APPROVAL ALREADY COMMITS EXACTLY 8 DECISION LEGS, AND 8 IS THE STORE'S HARD MAXIMUM.

Measured with a logging Proxy over `store.commitExpectedVersionDecisionLegs` bound to the real store, driving `approvePlan` over the production `boundWorld -> committedRevision -> approveGate1 -> submit` path — the same path `journeyWorld` takes:

    legs 8: [goal-1, moe-budget-ledger root, run-1, planning-authority/run-1, project-1-policy,
             policy-run-evaluation:run-1, active-graph-slot:project-1, session-authority/replay]
    a 9th leg -> DurableStoreError: STORE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED: legs cannot exceed 8 elements

The budget on `activateInitialGraphWithApprovalReplay` is fixed: 1 primary (goal) + 1 GENESIS budget root + N risk legs + 5 source fences (`approval-intent-source-fences.ts:59-65` — run, planning-authority, project-policy, run-policy, active-graph-slot) + 1 replay marker. `slotFenceLegs` is already `[]` on this path because `approvalSourceFences !== undefined`. So N MUST BE 0.

WHY THIS BINDS THIS ROW SPECIFICALLY. N is 0 today only because the risk leg is ALWAYS refused here — `readCurrentActiveGraph` answers ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT, the subject is null, and `buildPolicyRiskLeg` refuses POLICY_RISK_SUBJECT_UNAVAILABLE. That refusal is not merely an observability gap; it is what keeps this decision under the ceiling.

**So if this row answers YES — plan approval should leave an active graph revision — the subject stops being null, the risk leg BUILDS, N becomes 1, the ordinary journey commits 9 legs and THROWS.** A "yes" answer therefore cannot be implemented by activating the revision alone. It must first resolve the leg budget, and that is a real architectural question rather than a detail:

    - reduce the five source fences (are all five needed on this path, or can any be folded?)
    - raise MAX_DECISION_LEGS with an explicit concurrency argument. Note the cap is deliberate:
      `packages/store/src/decision-legs-contracts.ts:3-8` says "Kept small on purpose: every leg
      costs one more version probe and one more receipt inside the single write transaction, so an
      unbounded list would hold the write lock for an unbounded time." Raising it is a store-wide
      tradeoff, not a local fix.
    - split the approval decision so the risk authority rides a different commit — which breaks the
      atomicity argument at `policy-risk-leg.ts:122-126` and must be argued, not assumed.

A "NO" ANSWER IS UNAFFECTED and stays cheap: nothing changes, and the row documents ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT-after-approval as intended with an arm pinning the code and layer.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR PLANNING THIS ROW: the two answers are no longer symmetric in cost. Whoever plans it should establish the leg budget FIRST — re-run the probe, confirm the count at HEAD — because that number decides whether "yes" is a one-row change or a two-row change. Do not discover it at step 4 the way c7a66b70 did.

ALSO RELEVANT: c7a66b70's own design was replanned because of this same ceiling. Its absence-marker leg was the 9th leg. Its replacement records the diagnosis off-ledger through an optional `HandlerContext` member instead. If this row makes the risk leg build, revisit whether that off-ledger workaround is still the right shape or whether the record can finally be durable.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
THE OWNER DELEGATED THIS DECISION TO THE ARCHITECT ("U decide i have no idea"), so the answer below is mine and the reasoning is recorded for anyone who wants to overturn it.

THE ANSWER IS NO: plan approval should NOT leave an active graph revision.

I LEANED THE OTHER WAY FIRST, and the measurement flipped me. `graph-revision-activation-leg.ts:15-21` quotes `graph-revision-reducer.ts:11-15` - "Initial activation is therefore THREE reducer results the daemon must commit in one atomic transaction" - and records that `readCurrentActiveGraph` "could never answer for a real project; every graph-revision history in the tree was written by a test fixture". Combined with the approval entry points being NAMED `activateInitialGraph` / `activateInitialGraphWithApprovalReplay`, that reads like an incomplete initial activation. It is not.

WHAT DECIDED IT, in two greps I should have run before forming the lean:
1. `daemon-command-graph-edges.ts:26` is a routing table and it says `graph.approve -> activateApprovedGraph (task-eacea969)`. There is ALREADY a command that owns activating a graph revision, wired at `daemon-command-graph-approve.ts:168`, and on that surface `graph-activation-service.ts:240-243` states "The revision leg is ALWAYS present - an activation that activates no graph is not a state this surface can express."
2. The journey NEVER RUNS IT. `git grep 'graph\.approve\|graphApprove'` over `gates-journey-fixtures.ts` and `gates-unattended-fixtures.ts` returns ZERO hits.

So ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT on the ordinary journey does not mean approval forgot to activate. It means the journey never ran the command that activates. The deleted fixture that FABRICATED a revision was papering over a missing journey step, not over a missing approval leg. The two surfaces are separate on purpose: `graph.approve` transitions the graph; plan approval's durable effect is `GoalExecutionEnabled` on the GOAL. Making approval activate too would put current-graph authority in two commands.

REJECTED - YES. It would expand `approval.decide`'s authority to move the active-graph projection that fifteen production sites read, to fix a symptom whose real cause is a journey that never calls `graph.approve`. Nobody asked for that expansion and no consumer has been shown to need it.

Filing a row on an unmeasured judgement is how this epic got its wrong cross-row constraint tonight. THE ARM CAN PASS FOR THE WRONG REASON, and this is the main risk because an ABSENCE assertion is the easiest thing in the world to satisfy accidentally. It stays green if the world was never built, if the approval silently refused, or if the read was never reached. Step 5 requires asserting the approval COMMITTED in the same arm and step 6 requires proving the arm reds when a revision IS present. Without both, this row ships a test that asserts nothing and looks like coverage - which is the exact failure class its parent row was filed to end.

THE DECISION CAN BE OVERTURNED BY STEP 2 AND THAT IS BY DESIGN. If the fifteen-reader classification finds a production reader that is genuinely broken or dead under ACTIVE_GRAPH_ABSENT - not merely fail-closed - then absence is not a benign intended state and the NO answer is wrong. The instruction is report_blocked, NOT a quiet switch to YES: changing the answer mid-row would make a product decision the owner delegated to the architect, not to the worker.
